Introduction & Executive Summary** ###### **1.1 Introduction** During the three months that passed since the release of our previous 3-Year Copper Forecast, prices have staged an impressive rally, on 11th November reaching an all-time-high, on an intra-day basis. Interestingly, this has happened during a time of considerable uncertainty towards the outlook for mature economies on both sides of the Atlantic. In Europe, those sovereign debt concerns that had subsided somewhat in the summer have re-emerged, pushing problemcountries’ yields back to the peak levels noted in May. Moving to the United States, unemployment remains high, the housing market continues to struggle and economic growth seems to be failing to meet expectations. Interestingly, as we note in Chapter 2, contrasting this seemingly uninspiring macroeconomic backdrop, most segments of the economy that are relevant to copper (and other industrial commodities) have tended to perform well over the period in mature markets. Most importantly, expectations that China would experience a notable slow-down in industrial production and, by implication, copper consumption have been proven wrong. These factors have resulted in healthy copper consumption growth. Against a backdrop of structurally contained and indeed slower than planned production growth, this saw the market move into deficit in the third quarter, according to GFMS’ estimates, which seems to have persisted and even increased in October and November. Coupled with the clearly bullish outlook for copper’s medium to long term fundamentals, the above have continued to fuel investor demand. The strength of the wider commodity sector has also contributed to this. Regarding the latter, as we discuss later in the investment section of this chapter, the most important event over the last few months has been the run-up and announcement of a new round of quantitative easing by the United States monetary authorities. This rise of investor interest in the red metal once again precipitated a rally which the fundamentals, albeit strong, could not have driven on their own. We continue to expect conditions worsening somewhat in the first half of 2011, as mature economies’ economic problems, relating to fiscal imbalances and problematic labour markets in mature economies, finally affect industries relevant to copper. Chinese authorities’ persistent need to keep inflation under control could add further pressure. At the same time, we believe that the price correction that ensues will be limited, as bargain-hunting consumers and investors will be quick to absorb the little excess metal in the market. Importantly, as a more sustainable path to recovery is entered later in the year, copper demand is expected to once again start trending upwards, resulting in a return to deficit and a rising price environment. From that point onwards, GFMS expect the copper market will remain in deficit throughout the rest of the forecast period. As we discuss in detail towards the end of this chapter, we have reached that conclusion even after allowing for healthy increases in production (growth in both years are forecast well above the average of the previous decade) and consumption being affected by substitution and thrifting. In addition to this tightness in the fundamental market, we are confident that investors will remain active in the commodities space with a long bias and that copper will remain one of the favourites. **4** Independent - Informed - International 3-Year Copper Forecast - November 2010 **CONFIDENTIAL** ###### **1.2 Economic Assumptions** As noted in the introduction, the recent copper price rally has come at a time when a number of headline indicators for the global economy have remained problematic and their outlook has been questionable. Despite this fact, the nature of the various stimulus packages around the world has meant that the manufacturing sector has tended to perform well, underpinning copper demand. Elsewhere, US dollar weakness has provided essential support, through boosting investor interest in “hard” assets. Going forward, our projections for the copper market are linked to our economic outlook. GFMS’ projections for the forecast period are presented in the form of three probability-weighted scenarios. Since our August forecast, the probability of our Base Case Scenario has remained at 50%. We have increased the probability of our high case scenario (Scenario

B) to 30% in line with the fact that further quantitative easing has been enacted in the United States and Japan. In contrast, the probability of our low GDP growth variant (Scenario C) has been lowered to 20%. **Base Case Scenario** (with a 50% probability outcome): Our projections for the global economy in 2010 have been revised higher since our last report. Accordingly, we now forecast world GDP growth to be 3.7% in 2010, up from 3.3% in our August forecast. Despite this, our Base Case Scenario remains cautious in terms of the outlook for 2011 and 2012 because of the indebted nature of both governments and consumers in much of the developed world. As the artificial stimulus of deficit spending starts to be withdrawn and inventory adjustment ends, GDP growth is set to slow in both the United States and Europe. Next year, the fuller consequences for China of the tightening of monetary and fiscal policies (such as potential weakness in the housing market), as well as slowly growing export markets, will be felt and growth is forecast to average 8.5%. Moreover, by this time the yuan should be slightly stronger against the US dollar and that, at the margin, should temper the increase in exports and encourage imports. In 2012 and 2013, we expect a marginal improvement in China’s GDP growth rate, which is based on the absence of further tightening measures being necessary then for the economy. In light of this, we expect a marked deceleration in global GDP growth in the first half of 2011 which, despite improvements in the second half, results in a global growth figure now forecast at 2.2%. This is followed by faster growth in 2012 and 2013 as the more traditional sources of growth, such as consumer spending, start to improve. The latter will be aided by unemployment beginning to slowly recede, albeit from elevated levels. **Scenario B** (with a 30% probability outcome): This is our most bullish view of the world economy, has global GDP growth averaging 3.6% in 2011-2013, after reaching 4% this year. Critical to this view is a very slow or in some cases non-existent withdrawal of fiscal stimuli and, from a monetary perspective, further substantial quantitative easing. Against this hugely accommodative backdrop, we believe it would become imperative for the United States to take measures by 2012, as US government bond yields would otherwise be forced to unacceptable levels. As a result, GDP growth is forecast to moderate in 2012 to an average of 2.6% before recovering slightly in 2013. LME Stocks vs Monthly Average Price

Accordingly, many advanced economies border on deflation, or at least disinflation. Global GDP growth is projected to be just 1.4% next year, with developed economies notably underperforming even that meagre result. Indeed, advanced economies’ industrial production is forecast to contract in 2011. In 2012 and further still in 2013, growth rates improve but remain historically low, especially for a post-recession phase of economic growth. ###### **1.3 The Dollar** The US dollar appreciated by over a fifth against the euro between December 2009 and June 2010, subsequently weakened by more than 15% and, more recently, has recovered some of the ground it lost. These swings have highlighted both the present instability of global currency markets and changes in sentiment regarding which major currency is viewed most unfavourably. These major swings in currency valuations and market sentiment illustrate the difficulty in forecasting exchange rates. Nevertheless, basis mainly its current purchasing power parity (PPP) undervaluation, we would expect the US dollar to strengthen against the euro over much of the forecast period. That said, we forecast that in terms of annual average dollar:euro exchange rates, in 2011 the dollar will be slightly weaker than the average rate this year at $1.39/€, in part due to the US Federal Reserve enacting further quantitative easing. From 2012 onwards we forecast a secular appreciation in the US dollar (against most currencies) under our Base Case. Besides the convergence towards long run PPP referred to above, this move will be assisted by the fact that by then the Federal Reserve will, finally, start to raise interest rates from their current exceptionally low levels. For 2012 and 2013, we project average rates of 1.37 and 1.31 respectively. ###### **Other scenarios** As regards the US dollar under our bullish Scenario B, the inflationary environment and lack of withdrawal of monetary stimulus will see a weake

ning of the American currency, at least on an annual average basis. Accordingly the euro is projected to strengthen from $1.43/€ in 2011 to average $1.47/€ in 2012. (Implicit in this scenario is that the European sovereign debt crisis does not deteriorate sufficiently to undermine the single currency.) By the final year of our forecast, the dollar is forecast to strengthen marginally as US interest rates start to rise. In the case of copper, where the overwhelming bulk of activity is essentially unreported, the task becomes ever more difficult. Nevertheless, using what limited data is available and combining that with anecdotal information, which we obtain through field research, conclusions on the direction and relevance of investor activity in copper can be reached. As we alluded to earlier in the chapter, investors have continued to be key drivers of copper price fluctuations, even if the motives behind their activities are rooted in the red metal’s fundamentals. Speculative positions in Comex futures have recently rocketed to levels unseen since the beginning of the year. Elsewhere, rising volumes and, particularly, open interest on the LME are also in line with this. Looking at Comex activity in some detail, the graph at the bottom right of this page features weekly investor positions in copper futures listed on the exchange. The figures are calculated using the disaggregated open interest data distributed by the CFTC and includes aggregated net positions for all classes of trading institutions/individuals reported on, excluding “Producer/Merchant/Processor/User”. As can be seen in the chart, the aggregate net long (which is understood to proxy investor positions on the exchange) has trended upwards during the last few months, peaking at 71,850 contracts, equivalent to nearly 815,000 tonnes on 9th November, up 261,000 tonnes on the end-July level. LME futures

open interest peaked at just over 310,500 contracts on 12th November, compared to just under 267,000 contracts and end-July. Given a lack of disaggregated data, it is not possible to be sure what portion of this increase is attributable to speculation and what to commercials hedging the price exposure of future consumption, but the trend is certainly in line with our contention that investor longs have grown. Copper investment demand over the last few months has also come through inflows into commodity index funds. As illustrated in the graph below, CFTC estimates of holdings of such funds saw them increase by $21.1 billion over the third quarter to reach $181.7 billion. The Commission has started publishing this data on a monthly basis and it is worth noting that in September alone, holdings increased by $21.4 (more than offsetting a decline in August). Two main forces have underpinned investor interest in copper over the last few months, the second round of quantitative easing and the market’s improving fundamentals. Regarding the former, for some time now the markets had been attributing a growing probability to the Federal Reserve entering a new round of quantitative easing and committing to perpetuating the low interest rate environment for the foreseeable future. On the one hand this was due to investors expectations that such policy would have positive implications for the market’s fundamentals. On the other, this is due to its fuelling inflationary expectations, which benefit investing in “hard” assets such as commodities. Copper’s long-term fundamentals have for some time been a key driver of inve

stment demand in the metal. As we noted earlier, since the summer it has been increasingly clear that what previously was an expectation had become reality, with downstream producers reporting stronger than expected results and production growth clearly lacking the required momentum to offset this. This undoubtedly fuelled speculators with excitement and has contributed to the recent rally. More importantly, GFMS believe that copper’s fundamentals have protected its price from corrections. For instance, we were not surprised to see that during the recent liquidation, triggered by the resurfacing of sovereign debt concerns, as Ireland was deciding whether or not to seek for external help, copper saw the smallest correction from its peak among the six main LME metals. Finally, copper investment demand benefited from growing rumours around the time of LME week of a number of institutions preparing (some having filed preliminary prospectuses) ETFs or other similar products which are backed by physical metal. The launch and success of such products would undoubtedly boost copper prices, as it would essentially remove part of the available stockpile of metal from the market. As Commodity Index Investments

GFMS continue to stand by our view that, even if such a suite of products does indeed launch, they will not necessarily be very successful with investors. This is primarily due to our expectation that management fees will be less favourable than other forms of copper investment and that this will act as a deterrent. Regardless of whether copper ETFs become a feature of the market, GFMS are confident that investors will continue to have a strong presence going forward. Our long term projections for copper investment are virtually unchanged from the previous edition of this report and we expect long-sided investor interest on the red metal to remain strong throughout the forecast period. Specifically, starting with next year (as the rest of 2010 is expected to continue on a similar note to the current one), we expect investors will react to worsening copper market fundamentals and a hike in risk aversion in the first half with liquidations. These will most probably be limited, as the correction that will ensure will be used as an opportunity by those to enter a market which they missed but also by some of

those that sold to re-enter with profits recorded. 

The recovery later in the year will undoubtedly be bought by investors, who will by that point also be more comfortable with risk, and this will augment the rally.  It will also result in high price volatility and we expect noteworthy, although probably short-lived, corrections to be frequent during the period.  Similar conditions are expected to be carried over to the final two years of the forecast period and indeed for as long as the copper market remains in deficit.  Investorbuying will continue to provide essential fuel for the price rally and this assumption has been instrumental in our forming the price projections discussed in detail in the final section of this chapter.

###### **1.5 Consumption** 

In line with the latest indications suggesting consumption growth has been faster than previously expected, GFMS have revised our copper demand projections for 2010 upwards somewhat, to show an 8.7% increase overall to just under 19 million tonnes. This comprises double-digit increases in a number of mature markets from last year’s low base as well as ongoing growth in emerging markets. 

Weaker economic conditions are likely to impact on copper consumption next year.  Mature economies, in particular, are expected to experience a notable slow down in the first half and Chinese demand could be affected by tightening monetary and fiscal policy. As such, even allowing for a notable recovery in the second half of the year, global copper consumption growth is forecast to slow to 3.9% in 2011. 

In the final two years of our forecast period, we expect projecting global consumption growth to slow.  On the one hand this is due to cyclical and secular factors, the former relating to growth rates in mature economies moving towards trend and the latter being a simple reflection of an every growing base in emerging markets.  In addition to these factors, GFMS expect that sustainably high copper prices will accelerate substitution trends and result in increased thrifting. 

As such, under our Base Case, GFMS are forecasting global demand growth to slow to 3.4% in 2012 before decelerating further to 3.1% in 2013, by which time global consumption will have reached 21.053 million tonnes.  On a regional basis, although we expect growth in the BRICs to ease somewhat over this period, the engines of copper consumption growth will remain within this group and other emerging countries.  By the final year of the forecast period, BRICs demand will account for 47%, compared to 44% last year. 

###### **1.6 Production** 

Our estimates for global copper mine production last year see output at 15.799 million tonnes, a 2.5% increase from the previous year.  Africa and Asia were the two principal contributors to the increase, the former due to capacity additions and expansions and the latter as a re

sult of increased output at Grasberg as well as modest growth in Chinese production. Continuing the recent trend, growth in SX-EW production exceeded that in concentrate production. The ongoing issues of lower grades and slower than expected ramp ups have led us to revise our projections downwards for 2011. Currently we are projecting a 1.8% year-on-year increase for the full year figure to 16.08 million tonnes overall. |

Allowances for lost and later on recovered output at First Quantum’s Frontier mine (as we discuss in more detail later on) have also played a part. We have extended our projections to 2013, during which year we expect production growth will slow to 2.3%, bringing the global total to 17.382 million tonnes. This is the result of a slow-down in African and American production, partly offset by faster growth in Asia. Our supply forecasts assume that mine production growth will not surge ahead despite our expectations of a very attractive price environment. The implication of our mine-by-mine analysis for r

efined production is that the latter will struggle to keep pace with demand due to limited raw material availability. We note also that this is based on fairly optimistic projections for secondary supply, in line with higher prices. We finally expect smelting and refining capacity to remain abundant throughout and that treatment and refining charges will continue to favour miners. ###### **1.7 Market Outlook** ###### **Base Case Scenario** We have revised upwards our forecast for the market deficit in the final quarter of the year to 151,000 tonnes (compared to 101,000 tonnes in the August edition), reflecting indications that consumption growth is set to grow faster than we had originally predicted and our view on refined production having been virtually unchanged from the previous edition of this report. We have also revised our price forecast, to reflect the rally towards the $9,000/tonne mark earlier in the month. In the first half of 2011, we continue to expect supplydemand conditions to worsen. In the first quarter, both production and demand take a seasonal hit. Demand is expected to see a bigger drop, affected by the economic problems discussed earlier and in Chapter 2. A surplus of 30,000 tonnes is forecast for the period, which is expected to be maintained, at a lower 20,000 tonnes, in the second quarter, when demand growth lacks momentum but refined output returns to current levels. Consumption accelerates in the second half of the year and more than catches up with supply, in spite of the latter growing at rates well-above trend. In the third and last quarter of the year, GFMS project deficits of 95,000 tonnes and 87,000 tonnes respectively. ###### **2.3  Economic Backdrop** 

Thus far in 2010 global growth has recovered somewhat faster than we had anticipated, given the underlying problems of many economies.  However, there are clear and growing signs that the slowdown we had forecast to take place thereafter is starting to occur, especially in the developed world.  This is unsurprising in our view given the unsustainability of government deficits, which have been crucial to the reflating of the global economy in the past twelve months or so.  The absence of further fiscal stimulus or, in some European countries, outright fiscal austerity measures in an attempt to avert, or manage, a sovereign debt crisis, is a key factor behind the deceleration in GDP growth in many of the advanced economies. 

In fact, although the sovereign debt crisis eased since the spring and the European stress tests were largely passed “successfully”, in recent weeks it has entered a new acute phase, with Ireland in particular seeing the spreads on its bonds over German ones rise to record levels.  Moreover, the austerity measures triggered by this year’s sovereign debt crisis have clouded prospects for decent GDP growth in Europe in 2011.  Meanwhile, across the Atlantic the latest economic data suggests that the risk has grown of an economic slowdown in the United States where consumer spending is constrained by elevated debt levels and high unemployment.

The drag from balance sheet rebuilding pushes down growth rates in **Scenario C** .  Accordingly, many advanced economies border on deflation, or at least disinflation. As a result, US GDP is anticipated to grow by only 1.3% p.a. for the 2012-2013 period. 

In Europe, the outlook also looks bleak as economic growth is restrained by the need to limit the increase in government debt and by high levels of unemployment that dampen consumer spending.  In fact, both the recent spate of austerity measures in this region plus an array of further steps to address the fiscal deficits could lead to EU-27 GDP increasing by a mere 0.3% in 2011.  Even accounting for a slight pick up in the growth rate thereafter, this means we forecast EU-27 GDP to still be lower in 2013 than it was in 2008. 

Given the difficulties faced by the Japanese economy over the past 20 years and its export driven nature, it is unsurprising that it struggles to avoid an outright return to recession under Scenario C.  Therefore, GDP is forecast to grow by a mere 0.4% in 2011, before there is a very modest improvement in the GDP growth rate in the final two years of the forecast. 

Countries that are more reliant on domestic demand during this period will perform better and, given the industrialisation taking place in many developing countries, they will continue to be the best performers. Needless to say Chinese growth will be the strongest among the larger countries in this group, although by its standards an increase of 8.0% next year would represent a fair dip.

###### **Europe** 

The general trend for capacity to be relocated to closer to the main sources of growth, coupled with a comparatively unfriendly environment to heavy industries (given the higher labour costs and polutionrelated legislation) are behind our only limited growth projections for refined production in the continent. The only major project expected to come onstream continues to be the Las Cruces operation in **Spain** .  Las Cruces’ SX-EW operation is due to reach full 72,000 tonnes by 2011, even though, as we noted in the mine section, technical problems have limited growth todate.
